html:
The Prague Spring was a period of reform in Czechoslovakia in 1968, begun when Alexander Dubček became head of the Communist Party in January, which ended when Warsaw Pact armies invaded on the night of 20 to 21 August.

Dubček promised socialism with a human face. Censorship was lifted, people debated freely, and the party planned economic reform and more rights. Moscow feared it would spread. About 250,000 troops from the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary and Bulgaria entered the country. Czechs and Slovaks resisted without arms, changing road signs and arguing with soldiers. Dubček was removed in 1969, and hard line rule called normalisation followed. In January 1969 the student Jan Palach burned himself to death in protest. Moscow's claim to a right to intervene was called the Brezhnev Doctrine. The hopes returned in the Velvet Revolution of 1989 during the Cold War's end.
sum: The Prague Spring was a period of reform in Czechoslovakia in 1968, begun when Alexander Dubček became head of the Communist Party in January, which ended when Warsaw Pact armies invaded on the night of 20 to 21 August.
